y-m-34-03.title: How many x values must equation hold at to prove it holds for all x?
y-m-34-03.topic: Identity: how many x values must make polynomial equation true to establish all x?
y-m-34-03.goal: As checking values one by one gives evidence, adjust confidence; connect number of needed values with polynomial degree.
y-m-34-03.material: a,b,c constants, equation ax²+bx+c=0. You learn one by one x values where it holds. Each step, choose if you can call identity (true for every x).
y-m-34-03.thinking.1: Understand why one/two values no proof
y-m-34-03.thinking.2: Generalize number of tested values vs degree
y-m-34-03.prereq.1: Difference between polynomial identity and equation (all x vs particular x)
y-m-34-03.s.s1.prompt: Information comes piece by piece. Choose judgment each time.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, put number of values checked beside expression degree.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.hint.1: Choose a,b,c yourself, e.g. make equation hold at x=1, then test other x.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.after: One matching value no prove identity or nonidentity. For example a=1,b=−3,c=2 works at x=1, but x=0 gives 2=0, false.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Identity, because it held at the value checked
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Any value can be a root, so one match doesn't say about other x.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Too early to be sure; that value might be a root
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: It can hold at root too. This considers if enough values checked.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Not an identity, because only one value checked
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You haven't shown it fails elsewhere, so no basis to say not either.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.after: If a=1,b=−3,c=2, holds at x=1 and 2 but not x=0. Even 2 values no certainty. Judgment same, but now clearer shape of possible counterexample.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Identity, because held at 2 different values
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: A quadratic can have 2 roots. Recall this possibility.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Unknown still. A quadratic can have two roots
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You compare checked values count with possible root count.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Not identity because it holds at only 2 values
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You haven't shown it holds only at 2; checking two differs from only two solutions.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.after: A nonzero degree≤2 polynomial has at most 2 roots. If equation holds at 3 different values, a=b=c=0 and holds for all x. Evidence now enough to change judgment. [0]
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Unknown. Need check up to a fourth value
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: More checks no harm, but degree≤2 means 3 values exceed max roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Not identity because only 3 values checked
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Three matches no evidence against identity. What if degree≤2 expression zero at 3 distinct points? [0]
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Identity. A degree≤2 expression cannot have 3 roots
y-m-34-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You conclude by comparing degree and checked values.
y-m-34-03.s.s1.reflect: How judgment change over 3 steps, and why? If same 3 values held but expression quartic ax⁴+bx³+cx²+dx+e=0, how should judgment differ?
y-m-34-03.s.s2.prompt: For degree 4 or lower polynomial P, how many different x values with P(x)=0 needed to conclude P identically zero? Choose smallest sufficient number. [0]
y-m-34-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think maximum number of roots quartic can have.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.a: x(x-1)(x-2)(x-3) equal 0 for 4 different values, but e no be 0 for all x. Quartic expression fit get four roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.b: If polynomial degree 4 get 5 roots, e become zero polynomial. This judgment apply rule 'degree + 1'.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.c: With 6 values e settled, but 6 no be smallest. E already settled at 5.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.r.d: 3 no enough. Quartic expression fit get up to 4 roots.
y-m-34-03.s.s2.explain: If polynomial degree n or below no be 0, e get at most n different roots. So if e equal 0 at n+1 different values, every coefficient na 0 and e hold for every x. For degree 4 or below, number na 5. Earlier, 3 for expression degree 2 or below follow same rule.

y-m-34-07.title: If a³+b³+c³=3abc, must all three numbers equal?
y-m-34-07.topic: Multiplication formulas: must 3 numbers be equal if a³+b³+c³=3abc?
y-m-34-07.goal: Use counterexamples decide whether claim 'if equation hold, all 3 numbers equal' true or false; check extra condition wey make claim true.
y-m-34-07.material:
For real a,b,c, one student make this claim.
Claim: If a³+b³+c³=3abc, then a=b=c.
Student check a=b=c=2. Since 8+8+8=24=3·8, equation hold. ('3abc' mean 3 times a times b times c.)
y-m-34-07.thinking.0: Separate direction of claim (condition and conclusion)
y-m-34-07.thinking.2: Find condition wey make claim correct
y-m-34-07.prereq.1: You no need memorize factorization of a³+b³+c³−3abc; you fit understand am when you see factorized expression
y-m-34-07.prereq.2: Cubes of real numbers and calculation with negative numbers
y-m-34-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose most suitable judgment about this claim.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.hint.0: Say in words which direction student check: 'if equation hold, numbers equal' or 'if numbers equal, equation hold'.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.hint.1: Test some small integers to see if equation fit hold even when numbers no equal. Put negative numbers too.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.a: It true because we confirm equation work when a=b=c.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.a: What we test na "if three numbers equal, equation holds." Claim na opposite direction.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.b: It true. Expression no change when we swap a,b,c, so dem must equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.b: Expression staying same when letters swap (symmetry) no mean numbers equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.c: It false. If numbers no all positive, equation no hold.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.c: You claim am without testing cases with negative numbers.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.o.d: Not known yet. Look for different a,b,c where equation still holds.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.r.d: You choose check yourself for cases wey break claim.
y-m-34-07.s.s1.explain: Claim says "always"; showing equal numbers work no enough. Test if equation can hold when numbers differ. Example (1,2,−3) works. 1 2
y-m-34-07.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different real triples (a,b,c) meeting a³+b³+c³=3abc with not all equal. Small integers easy.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.hint.0: Choose small integers, calculate both sides separately. Try negative numbers too. 3
y-m-34-07.s.s2.hint.1: When equation works, calculate a+b+c and compare across examples.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.ok.c2: The three numbers no all same.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The three numbers all same. A counterexample must have different values.
y-m-34-07.s.s2.explain: (1,2,−3): 1+8−27=−18; 3·1·2·(−3)=−18. Your examples all have sum 0. Since a³+b³+c³−3abc=(a+b+c)(a²+b²+c²−ab−bc−ca), sum zero makes equation true even when numbers differ. 0 1 2
y-m-34-07.s.s3.prompt: What condition can we add to make "equation holds means a=b=c" true? Choose all conditions that guarantee equality.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write a³+b³+c³−3abc as (a+b+c) times another factor; what must each factor be for product 0?
y-m-34-07.s.s3.hint.1: For each option, test with your examples whether condition and equation can both hold.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.a: (1,2,−3) is an integer counterexample meeting equation. 1 2
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.b: If all positive, sum cannot be 0; other factor must be 0, so numbers equal.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.d: If sum nonzero, other factor must be 0, then a=b=c. 0
y-m-34-07.s.s3.r.e: Sum of negatives cannot be 0, so numbers become equal for same reason as positives.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.explain: a³+b³+c³−3abc=(1/2)(a+b+c){(a−b)²+(b−c)²+(c−a)²}. If sum nonzero and equation holds, second factor zero, so a=b=c. All positive or all negative ensures sum nonzero. Integer or abc≠0 no prevent (1,2,−3). 0 0 0 1 2
y-m-34-07.s.s3.acc.0: Both conditions work. Also see broader condition: sum not 0.
y-m-34-07.s.s3.acc.1: You chose widest condition. Positive or negative also guarantee sum nonzero, same result. 0

y-m-34-04.title: Sum of cubes of two numbers whose sum na 5
y-m-34-04.topic: Multiplication formulas and sum/product of two letters: sum of cubes when only sum known
y-m-34-04.goal: Judge one step at a time whether a³+b³ get fixed value when only sum known and when both sum and product known; check your judgment with examples wey get same sum but different cube sums.
y-m-34-04.material: For two numbers a and b, we know a+b=5. We wan know value of a³+b³ (a³ na a multiply by itself three times). Check how judgment change as information come one piece at a time.

y-m-34-04.s.s1.hint.1: Choose 2 or 3 pairs wey sum to 5, calculate a³+b³ for each and compare.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Wetin you judge about value a³+b³?
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.after: Same sum no guarantee sum of cubes same too. Make only two exact pairs and compare to check.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Generally, sum of cubes of two numbers wey sum to 5 no be cube of 5. Expanding (a+b)³ show extra terms too.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We no know yet. We need choose different a and b and compare values.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This thinking make different pairs with same sum and compare dem.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: No fixed value dey. Two letters, but only one equation.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Conclusion correct, but you no always fit decide only by counting letters and equations. Make one example to check am make e more certain.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.info: It also known say a and b both integers.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now a³+b³ get one fixed value?
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.after: Even with integer condition, several pairs get sum 5. New information no change judgment, but e reduce possible cases to integer pairs. Make we check below.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: E don decide. With integer condition, a and b get one fixed pair.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Integer pairs with sum 5 keep going, like (1,4), (2,3), (0,5), (-1,6). Integer condition alone no reduce dem to one.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Maybe e no fixed. Several integer pairs get sum 5.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: Even though new condition added, you check remaining possibilities directly and keep your judgment.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: E don decide. Since dem integers, we fit find a and b straight away.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: With only one equation a+b=5, a and b no fixed as one pair either.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.after: (a+b)³=a³+b³+3ab(a+b), so a³+b³=125-3·4·5=65. Calculating with a=1,b=4 too give 1+64=65. When both sum and product known, value get fixed.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: In formula (a+b)³=a³+b³+3ab(a+b), this subtract only 12 for 3ab, without multiply by (a+b).
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: This come from subtracting 3ab(a+b)=3·4·5=60 from expansion of (a+b)³.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This still use only sum and no use product information.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This subtract ab(a+b)=20 instead of 3ab(a+b). Coefficient 3 left out.
y-m-34-04.s.s1.reflect: Across three steps, what information make you change judgment and what information no change am? If expression na a²+b² instead of a³+b³, sum alone decide am, or product too needed?
y-m-34-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 integer pairs a,b with a+b=5 and different a³+b³ values. (Pairs wey only differ by order count as same.)
y-m-34-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write how b get fixed once you choose a, then make table of some pairs.
y-m-34-04.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate a³+b³ for every pair and choose pairs wey give different values.
y-m-34-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Abeg choose a and b as integers.
y-m-34-04.s.s2.explain: (1,4) give 1+64=65; (2,3) give 8+27=35; (0,5) give 125; and (-1,6) give -1+216=215. All sums na 5, but cube sums differ. Since a³+b³=125-15ab, product ab change mean value change too.

y-m-34-06.title: Possible b in quadratic expression with constant term 12
y-m-34-06.topic: Factor quadratic expressions: possible linear coefficients when constant term na 12
y-m-34-06.goal: Check cases left out by conclusion 'we find dem all'; find different integer b values wey satisfy condition, and way to gather every one without missing.
y-m-34-06.material: For integer b, find every value making x²+bx+12 expressible as product of two linear expressions with integer coefficients, (x+p)(x+q). One student summarize below.
y-m-34-06.thinking.0: Find cases left out and point out overgeneralization mistake

y-m-34-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in this proof wey hard to believe. (Either cause line or conclusion line wey become hard to believe count.)
y-m-34-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, write what range from previous line its conclusion come from, and check whether that range cover full range question ask about.

y-m-34-06.s.s1.line.0: If we write x²+bx+12=(x+p)(x+q), then pq=12 and p+q=b.
y-m-34-06.s.s1.line.3: These 3 pairs na the only ones, so possible b only 7, 8, 13.
y-m-34-06.s.s1.explain: Lines 2 and 4 na problem. For line 2, p and q limited to 'positive integers', but if pq=12, both p and q fit be negative. For example, (-3)(-4)=12 and p+q=-7, so b=-7 possible too. So line 4 conclusion 'only these 3 pairs' no check missing cases. Lines 1 and 3 correct.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 4 different integer b values wey make x²+bx+12 expressible as product of two linear expressions with integer coefficients.

y-m-34-06.s.s2.fail.c2: For this b, no two real numbers fit have product 12 and sum b.

y-m-34-06.s.s2.fail.c3: For this b, no two integers fit have product 12 and sum b.
y-m-34-06.s.s2.explain: Integer pairs with product 12 na (1,12), (2,6), (3,4), and (-1,-12), (-2,-6), (-3,-4). Their sums na 13, 8, 7, -13, -8, -7, so 6 b values possible (±7, ±8, ±13).

y-m-34-05.title: If equation correct, dem go accept am as quotient and remainder?
y-m-34-05.topic: Polynomial division: condition to be quotient and remainder even when A=BQ+R hold
y-m-34-05.goal: Confirm yourself say several (Q,R) pairs fit satisfy A=B·Q+R; understand remainder-degree condition needed to accept dem as quotient and remainder; continue division by fixing answer wey no fit condition.
y-m-34-05.material:
Divide A(x)=x³+2x²+3x+4 by B(x)=x²+1. Three students say these answers, and all confirm 'A=B·Q+R hold'.
  Jimin: quotient Q=x+2, remainder R=2x+2
  Harin: quotient Q=x+1, remainder R=x²+2x+3
  Doyun: quotient Q=x, remainder R=2x²+2x+4
y-m-34-05.thinking.0: Separate expression identity from conditions on division result
y-m-34-05.thinking.1: Make several solutions and discover uniqueness come from convention
y-m-34-05.thinking.2: Continue from wrong answer to correct one
y-m-34-05.prereq.1: Expand polynomial products and add/subtract dem
y-m-34-05.s.s1.prompt: Make more (Q,R) pairs wey satisfy A=B·Q+R. Let Q=x+p, R=ux²+vx+w (p,u,v,w na integers); find 3 pairs different from all 3 student pairs, with different p values.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write Q=x+p, expand B·Q. If you subtract that answer from A, result suppose be R.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.hint.1: Change p by one integer at a time (skip values used by three students), calculate each R coefficient and make table.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.ok.c2: Coefficient of x² term match A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c2: When you expand B·Q+R, coefficient of x² no match 2 in A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.ok.c3: Coefficient of x term match A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c3: When B·Q+R expanded, x coefficient no match 3 in A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c4: When B·Q+R expanded, constant term no match 4 in A.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.ok.c5: Dem different from the pairs given by the three students.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.fail.c5: If p na 0, 1 or 2, na pair one of the students already give. Please choose different p.
y-m-34-05.s.s1.explain: B·(x+p)=x³+px²+x+p, so R=A−B·Q=(2-p)x²+2x+(4-p). p=2 na Jimin answer, p=1 na Harin answer, p=0 na Doyun answer; plenty more dey, like p=3 or p=-1.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.prompt: Even though several (Q,R) pairs dey, what convention we need to talk of 'the quotient and remainder of the division' as one answer?
y-m-34-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put pairs wey you make side by side and compare how Q and R differ between pairs.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.hint.1: Apply each convention in the options to pairs above and count how many still remain.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.o.a: Only accept pair whose Q degree lowest.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.r.a: All Q pairs you make na linear. This convention no remove any pair.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.o.b: Only accept pairs where degree of R less than degree of B.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.r.b: You choose agreement wey compare remainder degree with divisor degree.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.o.c: Only accept pairs where every R coefficient positive.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.r.c: At p=0 and 1, all R coefficients positive too, so several pairs remain. Instead, p=2 where u=0 get excluded.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.o.d: Only accept pairs where every R coefficient integer.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.r.d: All pairs you make get integer coefficients, so this convention no remove any.
y-m-34-05.s.s2.explain: With convention degree of R gats be less than B degree (2), x² coefficient gats be 0, so p=2, that is, Q=x+2, R=2x+2 na only pair wey remain. Without this convention, unlimited pairs satisfy equation. So when we state division result, we also say 'remainder degree less than divisor degree'.
y-m-34-05.s.s3.prompt: Harin say Q=x+1, R=x²+2x+3. Equation correct, so explain why hard to accept am as 'division result', then show how to get from Harin R to Jimin answer.

y-m-34-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Degree of Harin R na ..., so ...
y-m-34-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: You point out say R degree no be less than B degree?

y-m-34-05.s.s3.model.0: Degree of R=x²+2x+3 na 2, so e no be less than divisor x²+1 degree. E still fit divide further. x²+2x+3=(x²+1)·1+(2x+2), so add 1 to quotient to get x+2, remainder 2x+2.
y-m-34-05.s.s3.model.1: If remainder quadratic, you fit divide am once more by divisor, so work never finish yet. Divide R by x²+1: quotient 1 and remainder 2x+2; total quotient x+1+1=x+2, same as Jimin answer.
